summary: Compilers insert unused bytes between and after struct members so that each member sits at an address suited to the CPU, which makes `sizeof(struct)` larger than the sum of its fields and sensitive to member order. You need this to predict memory use, shrink hot data structures, and avoid bugs when structs are written to files, sent over networks or compared with `memcmp`. It matters in kernels, embedded firmware, protocol parsers and any performance work on arrays of records.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A C struct is not a packed bag of bytes. The compiler places each member at an address that suits the CPU and, to do that, inserts unused bytes called **padding** between members and after the last one. As a result `sizeof(struct)` is usually larger than the sum of the member sizes, and it changes when you reorder the members. Layout is decided by the platform ABI (the rules for a given CPU and operating system), not by the C language itself, so the same source can produce different sizes on different targets.
bullets: **Problem it solves**: hardware reads and writes memory most efficiently when an N-byte value sits at an address divisible by N.
**What you pay**: wasted bytes, which hurt cache density and memory footprint in large arrays.
**Where it bites**: binary file formats, network headers, shared memory, hardware registers, and any code that treats a struct as raw bytes.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Alignment**: the rule that a type's address must be a multiple of some power of two. `_Alignof(T)` (C11, `alignof` in C23) reports it.
**Natural alignment**: usually equal to the size for scalar types: `char` 1, `short` 2, `int` and `float` 4, `double` and 64-bit pointers 8 on x86-64 Linux.
**Padding**: bytes the compiler adds. Interior padding goes between members, tail padding goes at the end of the struct.
**Offset**: distance in bytes from the start of the struct to a member. `offsetof(type, member)` from `<stddef.h>` gives it.
**Struct alignment**: the largest alignment among its members. This is also the alignment of the struct's first byte, since the first member has offset 0.
**Struct size**: always a multiple of the struct alignment, so that every element of an array of structs is itself aligned.
**Packing**: asking the compiler to drop padding, for example with `#pragma pack(1)` or `__attribute__((packed))`. This is a compiler extension, not standard C.
**ABI**: the platform contract (System V AMD64, Windows x64, ARM AAPCS) that fixes type sizes and alignments.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: The compiler walks the members in declaration order, which the standard requires it to preserve. For each member it rounds the current offset up to the member's alignment, places the member there, and advances the offset by the member's size. After the last member it rounds the total up to the struct alignment. The rule for a member at running offset `cur` with alignment `a` is: offset = (cur + a - 1) & ~(a - 1).
bullets: Step 1: start at offset 0 with struct alignment 1.
Step 2: for each member, round the offset up to its alignment, record it, add its size.
Step 3: struct alignment is the maximum member alignment seen.
Step 4: round the final offset up to the struct alignment. That is the size.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Reordering**: sort members by descending alignment. Struct C and D hold identical fields, yet D is 8 bytes smaller. This is free and portable.
**`#pragma pack(n)`**: caps the alignment of members at n bytes (supported by GCC, Clang and MSVC). `pack(1)` removes all padding. Use `#pragma pack(push, 1)` and `#pragma pack(pop)` to scope it.
**`__attribute__((packed))`**: GCC and Clang attribute with the same effect on one struct. Taking the address of a packed member can yield a misaligned pointer.
**`_Alignas(n)` / `alignas`**: raises alignment, for example to a 64-byte cache line or a 16-byte SIMD boundary. It can only increase alignment, not lower it.
**Bit-fields**: `unsigned a : 3;` packs several small fields into one storage unit. Order and straddling rules are implementation-defined, so avoid them for wire formats.
**Unions**: size is the largest member rounded up to the largest alignment. There is no interior padding because members overlap.
**Flexible array member**: `int data[];` as the last member. It adds no size, though the struct may still have tail padding before the array begins.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Time**: layout is computed at compile time. Access cost is the same as any member access: a load at base + constant offset.
**Space**: struct C wastes 11 of 24 bytes (46 percent). An array of one million of them costs 24 MB instead of 16 MB for the reordered struct D.
**Cache**: a 64-byte cache line holds 2 elements of a 24-byte struct (with 16 bytes of the third) but exactly 4 of a 16-byte struct. Smaller structs mean fewer misses when scanning.

**Misaligned access**: on x86 it works but can cost extra cycles, and a load that crosses a cache line or page boundary is split in two. Older ARM cores and many MIPS or SPARC cores raise a fault. Atomic operations on misaligned data are not guaranteed atomic.
**Packed structs**: the compiler may generate byte-by-byte loads on strict-alignment targets, so a packed hot path can be several times slower.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Assuming `sizeof` is the sum of members**: it almost never is. Always print it.
**`fwrite(&s, sizeof s, 1, f)`**: writes padding bytes (garbage) and bakes the host layout and endianness into the file. Serialize field by field.

**`memcmp` or hashing a whole struct**: padding bytes hold indeterminate values, so two logically equal structs can compare unequal. Compare members individually or `memset` the struct first (but note that assigning members may still leave padding unspecified).
**Information leaks**: copying a struct with uninitialized padding to user space or to a socket can leak stack or heap contents. Kernels zero structs before copying them out for this reason.
**Casting a byte buffer to a struct pointer**: breaks alignment and strict-aliasing rules. Use `memcpy` into a local struct instead.
**Packed struct member addresses**: `int *p = &packed.i;` may be misaligned and is undefined behaviour to dereference on some targets. GCC warns with `-Waddress-of-packed-member`.
**Different ABIs**: on 32-bit x86 Linux `double` inside a struct has alignment 4, so struct C is 16 bytes there, not 24. On Windows `long` is 4 bytes, on Linux x86-64 it is 8.
**Hidden tail padding**: adding a `char` to a struct whose size is already a multiple of 8 can grow it by a full 8 bytes.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Network and file formats**: protocol headers (IPv4, TCP) are declared packed or parsed field by field to match the wire layout exactly.
**Hardware registers**: memory-mapped device structs rely on exact offsets, usually with `static_assert` on `offsetof`.

**Linux kernel**: `pahole` from the dwarves package prints holes in kernel structs, and developers reorder fields to shrink hot structures such as `struct page` and `struct sk_buff`. `____cacheline_aligned` separates fields used by different CPUs.
**Allocators**: `malloc` returns memory aligned for `max_align_t`, 16 bytes on x86-64 glibc, so any struct can live there.
**Game and database engines**: structure-of-arrays layouts and hand-ordered fields keep records dense for cache-friendly scans.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **What is the size of `struct { char c; int i; }`?** 8 on common 32 and 64-bit targets: c at 0, three bytes of padding, i at 4.
**Why does the compiler add padding?** So each member is naturally aligned for fast, possibly atomic, hardware access.
**Why is there tail padding?** So that in an array every element starts at a correctly aligned address.
**How do you shrink a struct?** Order members from largest alignment to smallest, or pack it if you accept slower access.
**Is packed portable?** No. It is a compiler extension and the result of unaligned access is hardware dependent.
**Can the compiler reorder members?** Not in C. Declaration order is guaranteed (C++ and Rust differ for some cases).

subtopics.title: Alignment rules by type
subtopics.summary: Each scalar type has an alignment that the ABI fixes.

sections.body: On x86-64 Linux (System V AMD64) the alignments equal the sizes for scalars. Pointers and `long` are 8 bytes, `long double` is 16 bytes with 16-byte alignment, `_Bool` and `char` are 1. A struct or array takes the alignment of its strictest element. On 32-bit ARM the AAPCS aligns `double` and `long long` to 8, while 32-bit x86 Linux only requires 4 inside structs. Always check with `_Alignof` instead of memorizing a table.

subtopics.title: The padding algorithm, step by step
subtopics.summary: A mechanical procedure you can run on paper in an interview.

sections.body: Take `struct { char a; int b; char c; }`. Offset 0 holds a (size 1). b needs alignment 4, so round 1 up to 4 and place b at 4, ending at 8. c goes at 8, ending at 9. Struct alignment is 4, so round 9 up to 12. Size is 12 with 3 bytes of padding after a and 3 after c. The same fields ordered as `int b; char a; char c;` take b at 0, a at 4, c at 5, then pad 2 to reach 8.

subtopics.title: Tail padding and arrays
subtopics.summary: Why size is rounded up to the struct alignment.

sections.body: Arrays place elements back to back, so element k lives at base + k * sizeof(T). If sizeof(T) were 13 with alignment 8, element 1 would start at offset 13 and its double would be misaligned. Tail padding fixes that. This is also why `sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0])` always works: there is no gap between elements beyond what is already inside the struct size. Nested structs behave the same way: an inner struct keeps its own size, including its tail padding, and the outer struct cannot reuse that tail space (in C; the C++ Itanium ABI can for non-POD types).

subtopics.title: Reordering members to save space
subtopics.summary: The cheapest and most portable optimization.

sections.body: Sort fields by alignment, largest first. Group `char` and `bool` flags at the end so they share one tail slot. For a record with a pointer, an int, a short and two chars, the naive order may take 24 bytes while the sorted order takes 16. Keep readability in mind: group logically related fields in comments, and add a `static_assert` so a later edit cannot silently grow the struct.
sections.code:
struct bad  { char a; void *p; char b; int n; short s; };  /* 32 */
struct good { void *p; int n; short s; char a; char b; };  /* 16 */

subtopics.title: Packing with pragma and attributes
subtopics.summary: Removing padding on purpose, and what it costs.

sections.body: `#pragma pack(push, 1)` forces members to byte alignment, so `struct { char c; int i; }` becomes 5 bytes. This is the usual way to mirror a wire format. Remember the costs: unaligned loads may be slower or fault, and the compiler generates safer but longer code when it knows a struct is packed. For protocol parsing the safest pattern is to keep structs natural and use `memcpy` or shifts to extract fields.

subtopics.title: Alignment control: alignas and cache lines

sections.body: `_Alignas(64)` (or `alignas(64)` with `<stdalign.h>`) places a variable or struct on a cache-line boundary. Two threads updating adjacent counters on one 64-byte line cause **false sharing**: the line bounces between cores even though the data is independent. Padding each counter to its own line removes the contention at the cost of memory. `aligned_alloc(64, size)` provides heap memory with the same property, and size must be a multiple of the alignment.
sections.code: struct counter { _Alignas(64) unsigned long n; };  /* sizeof is 64 */

subtopics.title: Bit-fields and layout
subtopics.summary: Sub-byte members and why they are not portable.

sections.body: A bit-field declares a width in bits, such as `unsigned flags : 3;`. The compiler packs neighbouring bit-fields into an allocation unit, but whether fields run from the least or most significant bit, and whether a field may straddle a unit boundary, is implementation-defined. A zero-width field forces the next field to start a new unit. Use explicit masks and shifts for hardware registers and network headers so the layout is the same everywhere.

subtopics.title: Padding, security and serialization
subtopics.summary: Uninitialized padding leaks data and breaks comparisons.

sections.body: Padding bytes are not part of any member, so a struct copy may or may not carry their old contents. If you send the struct over a socket, write it to disk or return it from a kernel interface, those bytes may expose secrets. Zero the object with `memset` before filling fields, or serialize each field explicitly with a fixed byte order. Do not use `memcmp` for equality unless the type has no padding, which you can assert with a size check against the sum of member sizes.

subtopics.title: Worked walkthrough of structs A, B, C and D
subtopics.summary: The four reference structs, field by field, aligned and packed.

sections.body: Adding member sizes naively gives A = 1 + 2 = 3, B = 2 + 1 + 4 = 7, C = 1 + 8 + 4 = 13 and D = 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. The compiler reports 4, 8, 24 and 16. In A, `short` needs an even address, so one pad byte follows the `char`. In B, `short` sits at 0 and `char` at 2, then one pad byte lets `int` start at 4. In C, seven pad bytes push `double` to offset 8, `int` follows at 16, and four tail bytes round 20 up to 24 so every array element is 8-aligned. In D the members are already ordered large to small, so only three tail bytes appear after `char` at offset 12. With `#pragma pack(1)` the sizes collapse to the plain sums 3, 7, 13 and 13, because no padding is permitted at all.
bullets: Normal layout: 4, 8, 24, 16 bytes.
Packed layout: 3, 7, 13, 13 bytes.
C and D hold the same members yet differ by 8 bytes, which is the whole argument for ordering by size.

sections.body: A processor fetches memory in bus-width chunks, for example 4 bytes on a 32-bit data bus at addresses divisible by 4. A 4-byte `int` at an aligned address arrives in one fetch. The same `int` at address 2 straddles two chunks, so the CPU performs two fetches and stitches the pieces together, or on stricter architectures raises an alignment fault. This is why a type's natural alignment equals its size and why padding is inserted rather than letting members land wherever the previous one ended.

subtopics.title: Where packing is required
subtopics.summary: External layouts that must match byte for byte.

sections.body: Packing is meant for data whose layout is dictated from outside: binary file headers (BMP and ELF headers, for example), network protocol headers, memory-mapped hardware registers and embedded-system record formats. In GCC you can use `#pragma pack(1)` or the `__attribute__((packed))` suffix on a single struct. Treat packing as an interface tool, not a general optimization. Pair it with `memcpy` into aligned locals when reading fields, and add `_Static_assert` on `sizeof` so a toolchain difference is caught at compile time.
sections.code:
struct __attribute__((packed)) bmp_pre { char magic[2]; unsigned size; };
_Static_assert(sizeof(struct bmp_pre) == 6, "packed");

takeaways: `sizeof(struct)` is the sum of members plus padding, and padding depends on the ABI and member order.
Each member sits at an offset divisible by its alignment; the struct size is a multiple of its largest alignment.
Ordering members from largest to smallest alignment usually removes most padding at no cost.
On x86-64: struct { char; double; int; } is 24 bytes, struct { double; int; char; } is 16.
`#pragma pack` and `packed` remove padding but risk slow or faulting unaligned access and are not standard C.
Never `fwrite` or `memcmp` a whole struct: padding is indeterminate and layout is host specific.
Zero a struct (`= {0}` or `memset`) before sending, hashing or copying it out, since padding bytes are indeterminate.
